title: Rotational Vacuum Friction of Nonabsorbing Particles
authors: F. Javier García de Abajo, Alejandro Manjavacas
abstract: A nonabsorbing particle rotating in vacuum can lose angular momentum only by converting mechanical energy into electromagnetic radiation. Here, we develop a quantum theory of rotational vacuum friction for small lossless particles and show that axial symmetry qualitatively changes the leading dissipation channel. At zero temperature, the frictional torque scales as $M\proptoΩ^7$ with rotation frequency $\ Omega$ in anisotropic particles due to the emission of correlated photon pairs whose frequencies sum to $2Ω$, while a contribution to the torque linear in $\ Omega$ is found at finite temperature. In contrast, axisymmetric particles are protected against photon-assisted friction regardless of temperature.
summary: This theoretical paper develops a quantum electrodynamics framework to calculate vacuum friction torque on rotating particles. It shows that this torque depends critically on particle symmetry and temperature, yielding distinct power-law scalings ($\Omega^7$ vs linear $\Omega$) depending on the thermal regime. The findings highlight fundamental symmetries protecting certain geometries from vacuum dissipation.
main_problem: The research develops a quantum theory to calculate the rotational vacuum friction torque exerted on small, nonabsorbing particles rotating in a vacuum.
main_result: The calculated torque exhibits strong dependence on particle symmetry and temperature; for anisotropic particles at zero temperature, the torque scales as $\Omega^7$, while axisymmetric particles are protected from this type of photon-assisted friction.
method: The calculation relies on applying Fermi's golden rule to second-order processes (two-photon emission/absorption) derived from an electric-dipole interaction Hamiltonian coupling particle excitations and rotation to the quantized electromagnetic vacuum field.
model_or_system: The system is a small, nonabsorbing particle with internal bosonic excitations ($\epsilon_j$) undergoing rotation ($\Omega$) in a vacuum at temperature $T_0$. The analysis uses quantum electrodynamics principles applied to rotational dynamics.
key_observables: Rotational friction torque ($M$), absorbed power ($P_{abs}$), and the scaling of these quantities with $\Omega$ and $T_0$.
important_parameters: Rotation frequency ($\Omega$), temperature ($T_0$) characterized by $	heta_0$, internal excitation gap ($\epsilon_g$), and particle anisotropy/symmetry.
main_assumptions: The particle is nonabsorbing (real polarizability); approximations are made regarding the relative magnitudes of $\Omega, 	heta_0,$ and $\epsilon_g$ to simplify the calculation into distinct temperature regimes.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the contributing physical processes (2PE, 2PA, PS) and plot the calculated absolute strength of rotational vacuum friction versus rotation frequency for various temperatures and particle shapes.
paper_structure: The paper builds from defining the interaction Hamiltonian and applying Fermi's golden rule to calculate transition rates. It then derives general expressions for the torque in terms of temperature-dependent sums, simplifying these into distinct asymptotic limits ($\Omega^7$ at low $T$, linear $\Omega$ at high $T$), and finally analyzing symmetry protection.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses open quantum systems dynamics by quantifying dissipation mechanisms (vacuum friction) that couple mechanical rotation to the zero-point energy of the electromagnetic field, which is a key area in advanced AMO physics and quantum optics.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. A small nonabsorbing asymmetric particle rotates about the z axis with angular velocity Ω. The particle can lose angular momentum through two-photon emission (2PE), two-photon absorption (2PA), and photon scattering (PS), all of which contribute to rotational friction. In particular, 2PE can occur at zero vacuum temperature, whereas 2PA and PS require a finite thermal photon population.

FIG. 3. Absolute strength of rotational vacuum friction in a nonabsorbing asymmetric particle. We plot the frictional torque as a function of rotation frequency Ωfor a prolate diamond ellipsoid with semi-axes of 100 nm and 76 nm at dif- ferent vacuum temperatures T0 (see labels). The vertical and horizontal dashed lines indicate the fastest mechanical rota- tion reported to date (Ω/2π = 6 GHz [48]) and the measured torque sensitivity in levitated nanorotors (∼1 × 10−27 N m [49]), respectively.

FIG. 2. Temperature and velocity dependence of rotational friction in nonabsorbing particles. We show different con- tributions to the torque Ms arising from the processes de- picted in Fig. 1 and dependent only on the θ0/Ωratio, where θ0 = 2πkBT0/ℏis the thermal frequency. The s = PS contri- bution is separated into terms associated with ±ℏmomentum transfers. The total torque (gray curve) is compared with the high- and low-temperature limits (broken curves).
